titre: The Tonlé Sap, the river that flows back toward its lake every year
accroche: In Cambodia, a 100-km channel flows toward the Mekong in the dry season, then reverses toward its lake with the monsoon: the lake at least quadruples in area.
contenu_vulgarise:
On a map of Cambodia, the Tonlé Sap looks like an ordinary tributary: a lake in the northwest, then a channel about a hundred kilometers long that joins the Mekong at Phnom Penh, at a place called Quatre-Bras. In the dry season, water from the lake drains through this channel toward the Mekong, as in any river. Starting in late May, it does the opposite: it flows back up toward the lake.

## The mechanism

The Mekong is more than 4,000 kilometers long and follows the rhythm of the monsoon. In late May, its level at Quatre-Bras reaches about nine meters, enough to push water back into the Tonlé Sap channel and reverse its current. The lake, which measures roughly 160 by 35 kilometers in the dry season, with a surface area of about 2,500 km² and a depth of less than two meters, then spreads over more than 10,000 km² (some sources go as high as nearly 16,000). It reaches about 300 kilometers in length and up to 14 meters in depth.

About five months later, around October, the Mekong has dropped enough for the channel to resume its original direction. The lake and the thousands of square kilometers of flooded plain drain out. An FAO report cites an estimate of 72 billion cubic meters of water stored this way each year.

## The shift

We picture a lake fed by tributaries and drained by an outlet. The Tonlé Sap works differently: it is a buffer reservoir for the Mekong, absorbing part of the flood and releasing it in the dry season. The direction of the current is not a property of the channel; it is the result of a comparison between two water levels.

That comparison is shifting. A study published in Nature Sustainability in November 2025 estimates that, between 1998 and 2018, the lowering of the Mekong riverbed cut the reverse flow by 40 to 50%. The authors attribute it to sand mining and sediment trapping upstream, whereas this decline had first been blamed on climate and dams. Their projections show the reverse flow reduced by 69% in 2038 compared with 1998. The calculated consequence: about 26 km³ more water flowing toward the delta during the monsoon, and a dry-season flow reduced by about 59%, which worsens saltwater intrusion.

What the study puts in question is not just the rain, but the level of a river's bed.

repere.texte: In late May, the Mekong's level at Quatre-Bras reaches about 9 m and reverses the current of the Tonlé Sap channel: the lake's surface area goes from about 2,500 km² to more than 10,000 km².
repere.source: FAO, Tonle Sap Fisheries: A Case Study on Floodplain Gillnet Fisheries (Lamberts, RAP 2001/11), part I

carte.punch: In Cambodia, a river changes direction every year: with the monsoon, it flows back toward its lake.
carte.idee: In late May, the Mekong flood pushes water back into the Tonlé Sap channel, which flows toward its lake: from 2,500 to more than 10,000 km². In October, the current reverses again. Sand mining cut this reverse flow by 40 to 50% between 1998 and 2018.

quiz.question: What reverses the current of the Tonlé Sap channel in late May?
choix: The Mekong flood, which rises higher than the lake and pushes water back toward it
Snowmelt from Tibet, which fills the lake from the north
Tides from the South China Sea, which travel all the way up to Phnom Penh
Rain falling on the lake's basin alone, which makes it overflow
quiz.explication: The channel's current depends on the difference in level between the Mekong and the lake: when the Mekong reaches about 9 m at Quatre-Bras, it pushes water back toward the lake. Rain on the lake's basin would instead make it drain toward the Mekong, and tides do not explain a five-month seasonal reversal.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the study published in Nature Sustainability in 2025, what caused the decline of the Tonlé Sap's reverse flow between 1998 and 2018?
choix: A drop in monsoon rainfall over the basin alone
Sand mining and sediment trapping upstream
The construction of a single large dam on the lake itself
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The authors attribute the decline to the lowering of the Mekong riverbed caused by sand mining and sediment trapping upstream, whereas the decline had first been blamed on climate and dams. Neither rainfall alone, nor a single dam, nor heat alone explains this figure.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How much water does the Tonlé Sap store each year, according to an FAO report?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: An FAO report cites an estimate of 72 billion cubic meters of water stored by the system each year. The 26 km³ figure belongs to a different estimate, the surplus projected toward the delta in 2038; the other two figures are made up.
